opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and honestly, I think both paths have value, but they answer different questions.

Specialized robots have been around for decades. Look at a car factory: industrial arms welding and painting with incredible precision and reliability. In warehouses you have sorting robots, and in homes you have robot vacuums. These work because the problem is narrowly defined. The environment is structured, the task is repetitive, and you can engineer around almost every failure mode. If your goal is to make money next quarter in one vertical, a specialized robot is often the pragmatic choice.

The limitation is that every new task means starting over: new hardware, new data, new engineering, new tuning. The cost of that long tail is enormous. And the real world, especially homes, offices, and hospitals, is unstructured. There are millions of slightly different tasks, and no single one is valuable enough to justify building a dedicated robot for it. That's why, after so many years of robotics research, we still don't have robots doing everyday chores in our homes.

So my personal bet, and I think a lot of the field is moving this way, is on general-purpose robots. The analogy I like is what happened in language. Before large language models, people built separate systems for translation, summarization, sentiment analysis, and so on. Then it turned out a single large model trained on broad data could do all of them, often better than the specialized systems. The knowledge transfers. Learning one task helps another.

We're starting to see early signs of the same thing in robotics. When you train one model on data from many tasks, and even from many different robot bodies, it generalizes better than models trained on a single task. It can follow new instructions, handle objects it has never seen, and use common-sense knowledge it picked up from internet-scale vision and language data. That positive transfer is the key reason I believe in the general approach.

That said, I don't think it's a strict either-or. In the near term, specialized deployments matter a lot, because they're where you collect real-world data, find real failure modes, and build a business that sustains the research. And a general-purpose model doesn't necessarily mean a humanoid that does everything on day one. It could be one foundation model that powers many different robots, each deployed in a specific setting, maybe fine-tuned a little. Generality lives in the "brain," while the deployment can still be focused.

The biggest bottleneck right now is data. Language models had the whole internet. Robotics doesn't have an equivalent, so we have to be creative: simulation, teleoperation, learning from human videos, and getting robots out into the world so they generate their own experience. Whoever solves the data flywheel will probably determine how fast the general-purpose vision becomes real.

So, short term, specialized robots are practical. Long term, I believe the general-purpose approach is the one that will actually bring robots into everyday life.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical tradeoffs, deployment strategy, and a personal long-term bet, but does not characterize arguments about the choice as philosophical.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it a lot, actually, because at Google DeepMind we've worked on both ends of that spectrum. My honest view is that it's not really an either-or question. It's more about timing and about where the learning signal comes from.

Specialized robots are winning today for a very simple reason: the problem is constrained. A warehouse picking arm, a surgical assistant, a robot vacuum. You know the environment, you know the task distribution, and you can engineer around the hard parts. That's why those systems actually ship and make money. And I don't think we should look down on that. Those deployments are also how you collect real-world data at scale, which is exactly the ingredient the general-purpose side is starving for.

Now, the reason I'm personally excited about general-purpose robots is what we've seen happen in language and vision. Once you train a single large model on enough diverse data, you get transfer. A model that has seen thousands of tasks learns the ten-thousandth one with much less data than a model trained from scratch. In robotics we started seeing early versions of this with projects like RT-1 and RT-2, and then with the Gemini Robotics work: the same policy can pick up objects it has never seen, follow instructions it was never explicitly trained on, and sometimes transfer across different robot bodies. That's a qualitatively different thing from a specialized system.

But I want to be careful here. The robotics data problem is much harder than the internet-text problem. There's no web of trillions of robot trajectories sitting out there. So the path I actually believe in is a hybrid one. You build a generalist foundation model, you pretrain it on everything you can get, including simulation, video, and data from many specialized deployments, and then you specialize it for a particular domain with a small amount of fine-tuning. The specialist becomes a thin layer on top of a generalist, rather than a product built from zero.

So if someone asked me where to invest, I'd say: if you're a company that needs to ship next year, build the specialist, but design it so the data you collect can feed back into something bigger. If you're a research lab, work on the generalist, because that's where the step change will come from. The two feed each other. I think in five to ten years the distinction will feel a bit like asking whether you should write a custom program or use a general-purpose computer. The answer will obviously be the general platform, with specialization on top.

r001.rationale: The response frames the choice as a practical question of timing, data, and deployment needs; it does not characterize arguments about the choice as philosophical.

astra-6.text:
I think the two approaches make sense at different stages. If you want to deploy a robot today, you need a well-defined task and an environment where it can perform reliably. Specialization makes that easier, and it gives you a clear way to measure whether the robot is actually useful.

But the longer-term opportunity is generality. We don’t want to develop an entirely new system for every task. Ideally, robots can share capabilities, transfer what they’ve learned, and adapt to new situations without extensive engineering.

So I wouldn’t treat this as a binary choice. You can start with a specific application while building a foundation that supports more tasks over time. The important thing is to deliver value in that first application, while making sure that what you learn helps you expand beyond it.

r001.rationale: The response describes the tradeoffs as practical and stage-dependent, but does not characterize arguments about the choice as philosophical.

sol-6.1.text:
I think these are two different time horizons. In the near term, it makes sense to build robots for specific tasks in well-defined environments. You can set clear requirements, measure reliability, and understand whether the robot creates enough value to justify its cost. Even a narrow application can be very challenging once you have to make it work consistently in the real world.

In the longer term, general-purpose robots are very compelling because we don’t want to engineer a separate system for every task. We want robots that can transfer what they learn and adapt to new situations. But a general-purpose robot still has to be useful at something concrete. Being able to demonstrate many tasks is different from performing those tasks reliably every day.

So I wouldn’t treat this as an either-or choice. I would start with specific applications while building capabilities that can be shared across tasks. The key question is whether solving each new application requires starting over, or whether the same underlying system makes the next application easier. That’s how specialization can become a path toward generality.

r001.rationale: The response frames the choice in terms of near- and long-term development and practical reliability, but does not characterize arguments about it as philosophical.
